readings.title: A messy lesson for the post-woke left
body: Today, Explained newsletter A messy lesson for the post-woke left Francesca Hong’s loss in Wisconsin shows how hard it can be for progressive candidates to outrun the politics of 2020. by Caitlin Dewey Aug 12, 2026, 8:30 PM UTC Gift Francesca Hong during an election night watch party at Atwood Music Hall in Madison, Wisconsin, on August 11, 2026. Talia Sprague/Bloomberg via Getty Images Caitlin Dewey is a senior writer and editor at Vox, where she helms the Today, Explained newsletter. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . Wisconsin won’t be the very first state to get a socialist governor, after all. In Tuesday’s gubernatorial primary, Democrats there narrowly selected David Crowley, a moderate county executive, over the democratic socialist and reformed Thanksgiving-hater Francesca Hong. This contest was widely seen as a test of the progressive movement’s strength beyond deep-blue cities…and a bit of a mess. Two candidates dropped out amid scandal just weeks before the election. Crowley himself suspended his campaign and endorsed another candidate, only to reenter the race with less than a month left. That teed up a chaotic, last-minute showdown between establishment Democrats and the party’s upstart left-wing contingent. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. That contingent was expected to win in Wisconsin, where Hong campaigned on practical issues like universal childcare, free school meals, and opposition to new data centers. But she also struggled to explain controversial positions that she staked out at the height of the pandemic — positions that both pro-Crowley groups and Republicans pilloried in well-funded attack ads. The furor certainly riled up Wisconsin Democrats: They turned out in huge numbers on Tuesday. And while Hong performed well in Madison and other liberal strongholds, voters in both Milwaukee and most rural counties went for Crowley. The Wisconsin primary was weird and messy, so I wouldn’t generalize its results too much. But there’s little doubt that Hong suffered from her association with “Woke 1” — a strain of early-2020s social justice activism that many on the left now want to disavow. You’d probably recognize Woke 1, even if you haven’t heard the term. More than a movement or a policy agenda, it was a strident, binary way of talking about race, class, and social justice that peaked after the racial reckoning of 2020…and that ultimately alienated many centrist and working-class voters, including some in minority communities. “Defunding the police” = classic Woke 1. So are calls to abolish police or prisons — or, as Hong proposed in one infamous 2020 tweet, to cancel Thanksgiving. Many Democratic voters agreed with the impulses behind these slogans — police and prisons need reform; colonialism bad — but felt alienated by the rhetoric around them. And even in Woke 1’s heyday, issues like immigration and racial justice mattered less to most Americans than things like healthcare and inflation. As left-wing candidates attempt to build new and broader coalitions, many seem to have gotten that message . Politicians like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed have both walked back comments about defunding the police, for instance. Instead, they’ve centered issues like affordability and healthcare and begun openly discussing how their positions changed. “There was a huge opening of the Overton window” during the pandemic, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said Sunday . “Rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.” ➨ Spend more intentionally. Frugality was all the rage in the wake of the Great Recession, when a generation of popular, thrift-focused bloggers taught Americans to do more with less. Pop culture has since turned on frugality, as a value — in part because people feel so pessimistic about their long-term economic prospects — but it’s still worth mining the old-school frugalsphere for relevant lessons . Did you know… that since 1980, the number of fires in the US has fallen by more than half? Thank more effective smoke alarms, automatic sprinklers, and fire-resistant furniture and finishes. Today’s trivia: Which German philosopher wrote Critique of Practical Reason ? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the country whose capital is Vientiane. That would be Laos , which — together with China, Cuba, North Korea and Vietnam — has one of the world’s only one-party communist governments. See More : Politics Today, Explained newsletter Francesca Hong lost. Here’s what it means for progressives. Take a mental break with the newest Vox crossword Why progressives are backing off “Woke 1” Everybody needs a personal AI policy. Just ask Hank Green. ##段落
《今日解说》通讯：后觉醒左翼的一堂混乱课

弗朗西斯卡·洪在威斯康星州的失利表明，进步派候选人要摆脱2020年政治阴影有多难。

作者：凯特琳·杜威 2026年8月12日，晚上8:30 UTC 赠送

2026年8月11日，弗朗西斯卡·洪在威斯康星州麦迪逊市阿特伍德音乐厅的选举夜观看派对上。塔利亚·斯普拉格/彭博社 via 盖蒂图片社

凯特琳·杜威是Vox的高级撰稿人和编辑，负责《今日解说》通讯。本文首发于《今日解说》，一份帮助你理解当日最重要新闻和故事的每日通讯。在此订阅。

##段落
威斯康星州毕竟不会成为第一个迎来社会主义州长的州。在周二的州长初选中，该州民主党人 narrowly 选择了温和派的县行政长官大卫·克劳利，而非民主社会主义者、改造后的“感恩节厌恶者”弗朗西斯卡·洪。这场角逐被广泛视为检验进步运动在深蓝城市之外影响力的试金石——而且有点乱。

##段落
就在选举前几周，两名候选人因丑闻退选。克劳利本人曾暂停竞选并支持另一位候选人，结果在不到一个月前又重新参选。这为建制派民主党人与党内新兴左翼势力之间的一场混乱、最后一刻的对决铺平了道路。

##段落

提交邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。

##段落
那支左翼势力原本被预期在威斯康星州获胜，因为洪在普适托育、免费校餐和反对新建数据中心等务实议题上展开竞选。但她也难以解释自己在疫情高峰期所持的争议立场——这些立场被亲克劳利团体和共和党人在资金充裕的攻击广告中大肆抨击。

##段落
这场风波显然激怒了威斯康星州的民主党人：周二他们以巨大规模出来投票。虽然洪在麦迪逊和其他自由派重镇表现不俗，但密尔沃基和大多数农村县的选民都投向了克劳利。

##段落
威斯康星州的初选既怪异又混乱，所以我不愿过度概括其结果。但毫无疑问，洪因与“觉醒1.0”的关联而受损——“觉醒1.0”是2020年代初期社会正义行动主义的一股潮流，如今许多左翼人士都希望与之划清界限。

##段落
即使你没听过这个词，大概也认得“觉醒1.0”。它与其说是一场运动或政策议程，不如说是一种关于种族、阶级和社会正义的尖锐而二元化的言说方式，在2020年种族清算后达到顶峰——最终疏远了许多中间派和工薪阶层选民，包括部分少数族裔社区。“削减警察经费”就是典型的“觉醒1.0”。

##段落
因此，呼吁废除警察或监狱，或者如洪某在2020年一条臭名昭著的推文中提议的那样取消感恩节，也纷纷出现。许多民主党选民认同这些口号背后的冲动——警察和监狱需要改革，殖民主义是坏的——但对其中的言辞感到疏离。即使在“觉醒1.0”的全盛时期，对大多数美国人来说，移民和种族正义等问题的重要性也不如医疗保健和通货膨胀。随着左翼候选人试图建立更广泛的新联盟，许多人似乎已领会了这一信息。例如，纽约市市长候选人佐赫兰·马姆达尼和密歇根州参议员候选人阿卜杜勒·埃尔-赛义德都已收回关于削减警察经费的言论。相反，他们将重点放在可负担性和医疗保健等问题上，并开始公开讨论自己的立场如何转变。“疫情期间，奥弗顿之窗出现了巨大的开放，”纽约州众议员亚历山大·奥卡西奥-科尔特斯周日表示，“那时的言辞不是我们今天会使用的言辞。”

##段落
➨ 更加有意识地消费。在大萧条之后，节俭风靡一时，那一代流行的节俭博主教会了美国人如何用更少的资源做更多的事。此后，流行文化转向反对节俭作为一种价值观——部分原因是人们对长期经济前景感到悲观——但仍然值得从老派的节俭领域挖掘相关教训。你知道吗……自1980年以来，美国的火灾数量下降了一半以上？这要归功于更有效的烟雾报警器、自动喷水灭火系统以及防火家具和装饰材料。今日冷知识：哪位德国哲学家撰写了《实践理性批判》？（你可以在Vox的每日填字游戏中找到这个及其他脑力谜题。答案见明日版。）昨日冷知识：昨天我们问你哪个国家的首都是万象。那是老挝——它与中国、古巴、朝鲜和越南一样，是世界上仅有的几个一党制共产主义政府之一。

readings.title: Does Trump even have an agenda anymore?
body: Politics / Donald Trump / The Logoff Does Trump even have an agenda anymore? ﻿The president’s August doldrums, briefly explained. by Cameron Peters Aug 11, 2026, 10:00 PM UTC Gift President Donald Trump exits Marine One after landing near the White House on August 9, 2026, in Washington, DC. Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here . Welcome to The Logoff: August is famously a slow time in Washington, DC. It’s hot and humid, Congress is out of session, and everyone who’s still here generally wishes they were somewhere else. Even by that standard, though, President Donald Trump is having an exceptionally listless month. There’s a war in Iran, which is trapped in its nth cycle of almost-a-deal-any-day-now (a deal may really be coming, but signs today are less hopeful ). There’s Trump’s push for the SAVE America Act, which has long looked mathematically unfeasible, and which senators abandoned this past weekend. There’s all of that construction . And then, there are a number of “zombie” priorities — previously dead Trump agenda items that are coming back to haunt the news cycle. Here’s what’s still on the president’s to-do list: The Reflecting Pool: Late last month, the Justice Department dropped its felony case against a former Olympian accused of vandalizing the pool, which was actually the victim of shoddy contractor work and poor decision-making . Trump was not pleased at the time, and, on Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the White House is pressing the DOJ to bring a new case. Birthright citizenship: In June, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s attempt to end birthright citizenship via executive order as unconstitutional. Then, earlier this month, he issued a new, far narrower executive order trying to restrict birthright citizenship at the margins. As my colleague Ian Millhiser explains here , that order is likely unconstitutional, too, but Trump is trying anyway. Fed independence: Another June SCOTUS ruling curbed Trump’s immediate attempts to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook , whom Trump has accused of mortgage fraud . But Trump is still trying, notifying Cook last week that he was “considering” removing her, according to ABC News . The slush fund: Attorney General Todd Blanche committed to ending Trump’s sought-after $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” in order to get confirmed to the role. Now that he has been confirmed, though, it’s anyone’s guess whether the fund will stay dead . Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. My dad sent some very cute photos of a troupe of baby raccoons to the family group chat this morning, so I read this Atlantic article about raccoon domestication with great interest. As it turns out, they really might be on the path toward domestication. But, right now, they make terrible pets. Still, it’s a fun read, and you can find it here with a gift link. As always, thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow! readings.title: Trump takes aim at childhood vaccines
body: Politics / Donald Trump / The Logoff Trump takes aim at childhood vaccines Fewer vaccines, more uncertainty: What to know about Trump’s vaccines order. by Cameron Peters Aug 10, 2026, 10:20 PM UTC Gift President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in the Oval Office on August 10, 2026. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here . Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is trying to revise the childhood vaccine schedule. What’s happening? On Monday, Trump signed an executive order recommending fewer childhood vaccines, directing new vaccine research, and attempting to advance “parental choice” on vaccines. The new guidance substantially cuts the number of shots recommended for all children, from vaccines for 18 diseases to just 11 . Vaccines for rotavirus, meningococcal disease, the flu, and Covid-19 are all among those the order no longer recommends for all children. What does that mean for vaccine access in the US? For now, not too much. The order only issues recommendations, and as the Washington Post points out , many states have already elected to stop relying on federal vaccine recommendations. It’s certain to increase confusion over vaccine safety, though, and could throw up new administrative barriers for parents. Why does Trump care? Trump has long amplified baseless conspiracy theories linking childhood vaccines to autism; on Monday, he claimed that childhood vaccine doses are “the size of a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body.” (They are not.) Parts of the order directly reflect Trump’s personal hobbyhorses around vaccines, such as a recommendation to break up the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine into three separate shots; as the Post points out, those kinds of individual shots aren’t even commercially available right now. What’s the big picture? Monday’s EO doesn’t make any earthshattering changes, but it’s concerning to see vaccine policy — or at least policy recommendations — made from the Oval Office. And the order will have another impact: Trump’s attempts to dictate vaccine policy to states, combined with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s year and a half plus of meddling, will only serve to further demolish America’s splintered public health consensus . 政治 / 唐纳德·特朗普 / 《注销》 特朗普瞄准儿童疫苗 更少的疫苗，更多的不确定性：关于特朗普疫苗行政令你需要了解什么。作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯 2026年8月10日，晚上10:20 UTC 赠阅 2026年8月10日，总统唐纳德·特朗普和卫生部长罗伯特·F·肯尼迪 Jr. 在椭圆形办公室。吉姆·沃森/法新社 via 盖蒂图片社 卡梅伦·彼得斯是Vox的编辑。这个故事出现在《注销》中，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你在不让政治新闻主导生活的情况下了解特朗普政府。在此订阅。

##段落

欢迎来到《注销》：唐纳德·特朗普总统正试图修改儿童疫苗时间表。发生了什么？周一，特朗普签署了一项行政令，建议减少儿童疫苗数量，指示进行新的疫苗研究，并试图推进疫苗方面的“家长选择”。新指南大幅削减了推荐给所有儿童的接种次数，从覆盖18种疾病的疫苗减少到仅11种。轮状病毒、脑膜炎球菌病、流感和新冠疫苗都不再被该行政令推荐为所有儿童接种。

##段落

这对美国的疫苗获取意味着什么？目前来看，影响不大。该行政令只是提出建议，正如《华盛顿邮报》指出的，许多州已经选择不再依赖联邦疫苗建议。然而，这肯定会加剧对疫苗安全性的困惑，并可能为家长带来新的行政障碍。

##段落

特朗普为什么在意？特朗普长期以来一直在传播将儿童疫苗与自闭症联系起来的毫无根据的阴谋论；周一，他声称儿童疫苗剂量“相当于把一瓶汽水倒进一个小孩的身体里”。（事实并非如此。）该行政令的部分内容直接反映了特朗普个人对疫苗的执念，例如建议将MMR（麻疹、腮腺炎和风疹）疫苗拆分为三针单独接种；正如《华盛顿邮报》指出的，这类单针疫苗目前甚至没有商业化供应。

##段落

大局是什么？周一的行政令并没有带来颠覆性的变化，但令人担忧的是，疫苗政策——至少是政策建议——竟然从椭圆形办公室制定。而且该行政令还会有另一个影响：特朗普试图向各州强加疫苗政策，加上卫生部长罗伯特·F·肯尼迪 Jr. 一年半多来的干预，只会进一步摧毁美国本已四分五裂的公共卫生共识。

readings.title: The 7 types of people you need in your life to be resilient
body: The 7 types of people you need in your life to be resilient
When you say you have “work stress,” what exactly do you mean?

Chances are, you’re not talking about major things such as layoffs, fireable offenses or obvious wrongs; instead, it’s the small stuff that wears you down. Like the endless email chains that lead nowhere but swallow up an afternoon. Or the company leaders who hold long, closed-door meetings that put everyone on edge. Or being asked to work on a project that rubs against one of your beliefs or values.

Authors Rob Cross and Karen Dillon call these “microstresses” — those countless small moments that occur in every workday and drain you of time, energy and enthusiasm. For 20 years, Cross has been researching effective collaboration at different organizations. He saw that a primary source of burnout and overwhelm, even among high performers, was an endless barrage of these microstresses. However, he also found that roughly 1 person in every 10 he interviewed was what he dubbed “a ten percenter,” someone who can handle microstresses and still have fulfilling personal and professional lives.
In their new book The Microstress Effect , Cross and Dillon identify 14 common microstresses, along with tactics you can use to minimize them.
Here, they explain how your relationships can actually be a key part of your microstress tool kit.
Resilience doesn’t depend on ride-or-die friends who have your back at all times.

You can build resilience in small moments of authentic connection with a range of people in your life. Sometimes we need empathy, but then too much of it can lead us to wallow in self-pity and not take steps forward. At other times, we might need advice on a path forward, a new perspective or just the ability to laugh at the absurdity of life.
Here’s how you can find resilience in moments of microstress by reaching out to connections in your life and by making sure you have these particular types of connections in your network.

Sometimes when you’re going through challenges, you’re not necessarily interested in advice or guidance. You just want someone who will help you feel heard and validated. This kind of support also helps you keep your emotional balance and demonstrates caring.
• Seek out people who have common experiences or challenges
Loved ones don’t always fully understand what you’re going through, so look for people who have walked in your shoes.
Talk less, and listen more. Consider something as simple as starting with “That sounds really hard” and “I can imagine how difficult this is for you,” rather than defaulting to giving advice.
People who inspire you to see and pursue a path forward

Your relationships help in two ways: They give you actual models for moving forward and they can motivate you to move forward. They may also hold you accountable for actually doing something rather than just wallowing in self-pity.
People who are more resilient take advantage of others’ ideas to envision alternative routes forward. And by doing this rapidly in small moments, you keep microstresses from magnifying.

This role is more than just being a sounding board; these are people you count on to help you make the right call. Note which people in your network are good at helping you cut to the chase to make decisions — people who say things like “Don’t waste your time on that” or “If I were you, I’d just go in and ask for the promotion” — and lean on them for that purpose.

A truth-teller is someone you trust to be straight with you — and someone you won’t dismiss when they say things that are hard for you to hear. They are vital for resetting your perspective and getting you to see the bigger picture when it’s hard to.
People who provide perspective when setbacks happen

It can be easy to spiral into a panic when you’re faced with obstacles , but seeing events in a broader perspective can put them in a different, more positive light. This widening is sometimes referred to as de-catastrophizing. But it can require heavy cognitive lifting to do on our own. We tend to fare much better when we have others to help us step back, reframe and see our problems in a broader context.

Try leaning on a friend with little to no connection to your work. One particularly effective form of perspective we get from others is the “knock it off!” variety — someone’s blunt advice when you’re caught in a rut of overthinking, stressing or being self-critical.

When microstresses are battering you, build ties with people who help you remember your values. This person could be a friend who is unimpressed with your professional credentials but who cares about you as a person.
People who help you manage surges at work or at home

Think back to a time when you experienced a sudden surge at work — a late-breaking request from a key client, a difficult period because your team was short-staffed, a high-pressure presentation. How did you get through that rough patch?

If you’re like many people, you probably resorted to heroic measures to get it done. But working harder to survive surges at work or at home can throw everything off balance, undermining your sense of control over your life. A more resilient approach is to ask for help.
• Proactively help people in your network

Don’t wait for a crisis to ask people for help or to step in to help others, either. The support you offer can be as simple as making a point to talk up other people and giving credit where credit is due in public settings.

Make an effort to build relationships with people who will be eager to help you because their goals and interests intersect with yours. Look for shared goals with people that might not even be part of work. You might coordinate carpooling for your kids, for example.

Laughter activates neural pathways of positive emotions, ups serotonin levels and limits stress hormones like cortisol. This translates directly into how you can protect yourself against the sting of microstresses. Laughter can help you relax and reset to where you can think better, be more creative and just feel human.

Small moments matter when it comes to laughter. The ability to maintain virtual ties with friends who share your sense of humor and who can lighten your mood throughout the day or week is a genuine benefit to the always-on culture.

当你说自己有“工作压力”时，你到底指的是什么？
很可能，你指的不是裁员、可被解雇的过错或明显的冤屈这类大事；相反，是那些小事消磨了你。比如无休止的邮件链，毫无结果却吞噬了整个下午。或者公司领导开冗长闭门会议，让每个人都紧张不安。又或者被要求参与一个违背你信念或价值观的项目。

作者罗布·克罗斯和凯伦·狄龙称这些为“微压力”——每个工作日中发生的无数微小瞬间，耗尽你的时间、精力和热情。20年来，克罗斯一直在研究不同组织中的高效协作。他发现，倦怠和不堪重负的主要来源，即使是高绩效者也不例外，就是这些无休止的微压力冲击。然而，他还发现，他采访的每10个人中大约有1个是他所称的“十分之一者”，即能应对微压力同时仍拥有充实个人和职业生活的人。

在他们的新书《微压力效应》中，克罗斯和狄龙识别了14种常见的微压力，以及你可以用来减少它们的方法。
在这里，他们解释了你的关系如何实际上能成为你微压力工具箱的关键部分。
韧性并不依赖于那些无论何时都全力支持你的生死之交。
你可以通过与生活中各种人在真实连接的微小瞬间中建立韧性。有时我们需要同理心，但过多的同理心可能让我们沉溺于自怜而无法向前迈进。其他时候，我们可能需要前进道路上的建议、新视角，或者仅仅是对生活荒谬一笑的能力。
以下是你如何通过联系生活中的关系，并确保你的社交网络中有这些特定类型的关系，来在微压力时刻找到韧性。

给你同理心支持的人
有时当你经历挑战时，你未必需要建议或指导。你只想要一个能让你感到被倾听和被认可的人。这种支持还能帮助你保持情绪平衡，并展现关怀。
要做到这一点：
• 寻找有共同经历或挑战的人
亲人并不总是完全理解你所经历的，所以寻找那些走过你同样道路的人。
• 传递善意
少说，多听。考虑从简单的话开始，比如“那听起来真的很难”和“我能想象这对你有多难”，而不是默认……

到给出建议。

那些能激励你看到并追寻前进道路的人

你的人际关系在两方面有所帮助：它们为你提供了前进的实际榜样，并能激励你继续前行。它们还可能让你承担责任，促使你真正行动起来，而不是沉溺于自怜之中。

更具韧性的人会利用他人的想法来设想替代的前进路线。通过在小瞬间中迅速做到这一点，你就能防止微压力不断放大。

要做到这一点：

• 培养“果断决策”的顾问

这个角色不仅仅是充当倾诉对象；这些是你依靠来帮助自己做出正确决定的人。注意你人脉中哪些人善于帮你直击要害做出决策——他们会说“别在那上面浪费时间”或“如果我是你，就直接去争取升职”——并为此目的依赖他们。

• 找到你的“说真话者”

说真话者是你信任会对你坦诚的人——即使他们说出难以接受的话，你也不会置之不理。当你难以看清全局时，他们对重置你的视角、让你看到更广阔图景至关重要。

在挫折发生时提供视角的人

面对障碍时，很容易陷入恐慌的漩涡，但从更广阔的视角看待事件，能让它们呈现出不同、更积极的面貌。这种视角拓宽有时被称为“去灾难化”。但仅靠我们自己做到这一点，可能需要沉重的认知负担。当我们有他人帮助退一步、重新框定问题并在更广阔的背景下看待困难时，我们往往能表现得更好。

要做到这一点：

• 通过新透镜看世界

试着依靠一位与你的工作几乎没有关联的朋友。我们从他人那里获得的一种特别有效的视角是“别闹了！”类型——当你陷入过度思考、压力或自我批评的困境时，有人直言不讳地给你建议。

• 强化你的核心价值观

当微压力不断冲击你时，与那些能帮你记住自身价值观的人建立联系。这个人可能是一位对你的职业资历不以为意、但真心关心你本人的朋友。

帮助你在工作或家庭中应对突发高峰的人

回想一下你经历工作突然高峰的时刻——关键客户临时提出的要求、团队人手不足的艰难时期、高压的演示汇报。你是如何度过那段艰难时期的？

如果你和许多人一样，可能采取了拼尽全力的措施来完成。但为了在工作或家庭中挺过高强度时期而加倍努力，可能会打乱一切平衡，削弱你对生活的掌控感。更具韧性的做法是请求——

帮助。
要做到这一点：
• 主动帮助网络中的他人
不要等到危机时刻才向人求助或介入帮助别人。你提供的支持可以简单到在公开场合特意称赞他人，并在该给予认可时给予认可。
• 寻找目标一致的人
努力与那些因目标和兴趣与你相交而渴望帮助你的人建立关系。寻找与工作无关的共同目标。例如，你可能会协调拼车接送孩子。

让你开怀大笑的人
笑声能激活积极情绪的神经通路，提升血清素水平，并限制皮质醇等压力激素。这直接转化为你如何抵御微压力的刺痛。笑声能帮助你放松并重新调整状态，从而更好地思考、更具创造力，并感觉更像个人。
要做到这一点：
• 在虚拟空间中分享幽默
在笑声方面，小瞬间很重要。与那些分享你幽默感、能在一天或一周内让你心情轻松的朋友保持虚拟联系，对始终在线文化来说是一种真正的益处。
• 使用自嘲式幽默
自嘲能让人看到你真实、脆弱的一面，并在团队成员之间建立纽带。一位领导者描述了她在另一个部门与同事产生的摩擦。在激烈时刻，她的同事常常能巧妙地说出“嗯，我解释得真好！”来化解紧张，然后两人都会笑起来。

能理解人或职场政治的人
当我们为一句随口的话而苦恼，担心自己在错误的时间对错误的人说了错误的话，或反复检查邮件以确保没有无意冒犯他人时，微压力就会不断产生和重现。当我们有一个比我们更了解政治格局的值得信赖的盟友时，我们就能更有信心地定位自己的工作和努力——而不是不必要地为无关紧要的事情担忧。
要做到这一点：
• 与连接者建立联系
在每个组织中，都有天生的连接者，他们似乎认识其他办公室和部门的人，甚至可能与校友有良好联系。他们是理解政治的有力支持。
• 维护一个可求助的同事网络
这些人不一定是你的最亲密盟友，只需是愿意分享经验和观点的人。一家出版公司的一位新星表示，她经常向一位在公司工作二十年、即将退休的同事请教。“她和我并不是特别亲近，但她超脱于政治纷争之上。她有惊人的直觉和经验，而且慷慨地分享。”

她思考着如何处理截止日期，以及某些人对被排除在信息圈之外的反应等等。
鼓励你断开联系、好好休息的人
休息对我们发挥最佳工作表现至关重要。研究发现，当我们休息归来时，幸福感会有所提升，因为休息减轻了压力，缓解了情绪疲惫，并改善了精力水平。大多数“十分之一高效者”表示，他们与大家一起度过的休息时间带来了更显著的好处。如果我们与他人互动，就更容易停止对个人或职业微观压力的反复思虑。
要做到这一点：
• 与他人一起追求自我提升
一位科学家告诉我们，每年新年到来前，她都会列出一份所有计划阅读的书籍清单。但她很少能有所进展，直到她在工作场所加入了一个每月午餐时间聚会的读书小组。她不仅因此有了坚持阅读的动力，还开始与组织中其他部门的人建立了联系——这些是她原本不会遇到的人。
• 投资于扩展社交网络
“十分之一高效者”非常重视与那些与职业或个人生活并非紧密相关的社交网络保持联系。一位名叫卡罗尔的受访者加入了一个疫情期间在她所在小镇成立的本地户外咖啡小组。一位媒体高管加入了一个本地歌唱团体，那里她一个人都不认识，但她喜欢去参加，并成为这个她原本不知道存在的社区的一员。尽管她性格内向，但在歌曲间隙聊天和欢笑对她来说却很容易。
摘录自新书《微观压力效应：小事如何累积成大问题——以及如何应对》，作者罗布·克罗斯和凯伦·狄龙。版权所有 © 2023 罗布·克罗斯和凯伦·狄龙。经哈佛商业评论出版社许可转载。保留所有权利。
立即观看罗布·克罗斯的视频——属于TED“我们的工作方式”系列：
关于作者
罗布·克罗斯博士
罗布·克罗斯是巴布森学院爱德华·A·马登全球领导力教授，也是Connected Commons（一个由150多家领先组织组成的联盟）的联合创始人和主任。他研究高效组织内部的关系网络和高绩效者的协作实践已有20多年。他与300多家组织合作，接触了从一线到高管的数千名领导者，并确定了在组织各个层面和任何职业阶段培养充满活力、高效网络的具体方法。他是《超越协作过载：如何更聪明地工作、领先一步并恢复幸福感》一书的作者。
凯伦·狄龙是作家，曾任《哈佛商业评论》杂志编辑，并与克莱顿·克里斯坦森合著了三本书——

《纽约时报》畅销书《你将如何衡量你的人生？》、华尔街日报商业畅销书《与运气竞争：创新与顾客选择的奥秘》，以及Thinkers 50突破性创意入围作品《繁荣的悖论：创新如何帮助国家摆脱贫困》的作者。

body: Future Perfect The strange reason flu shots have been so hard to improve America finally has an mRNA flu shot. Now comes the fight to actually use it. by Bryan Walsh Aug 8, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Gift Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Bryan Walsh is a senior editorial director at Vox, covering AI and other subjects for the Future Perfect section and audio/video, and writing the Good News newsletter. He worked at Time magazine for 15 years as a foreign correspondent in Asia, a climate writer, and an international editor, and he wrote a book on existential risk. On August 5, 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services canceled 22 mRNA vaccine projects worth roughly $500 million and told the country it would stop investing in the technology that had brought us life-saving Covid vaccines. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine skeptic, claimed that the data showed these vaccines fail to protect against upper respiratory infections like Covid and flu. That his claims weren’t true — Moderna had already published Phase 3 trial results showing the opposite — didn’t seem to matter. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. On August 5, 2026 — one year to the day later — the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved mFLUSIVA , the first mRNA influenza vaccine ever licensed in the United States. That symmetry, while highly useful to writers like myself who are always looking to identify the rhymes of history, wasn’t planned. The approval landed on the one-year anniversary simply because of the deadline the agency had set for itself in February of this year, after it refused to review Moderna’s application and then, 15 days later, reversed itself . The decision didn’t earn a huge amount of press, in part because seasonal flu is a disease Americans have rarely taken seriously — fewer than 50 percent of US adults got their flu shot this past fall and winter. But flu is no joke: the 2024–25 season produced 51 million illnesses, 710,000 hospitalizations, and 45,000 deaths . That’s more than the number of Americans who died in car crashes last year. And the damage from a flu virus doesn’t stop when the fever does. In the week after a confirmed infection, the risk of a heart attack runs roughly six times higher than normal . So a better flu vaccine matters. But the more interesting thing is what the approval says about the year that produced it. The nine experts who voted unanimously that this vaccine’s benefits outweigh its risks were appointed under the very same secretary who was against mRNA technology. Asked to look at the evidence, those experts couldn’t produce a single vote against it. That’s not quite a change of heart, but at a dark time for public health, it’s something to hang our hopes on — because flu could just be the start for this technology. If you’ve ever taken a flu shot, thank a chicken. Every flu vaccine Americans have received since the 1940s has been grown inside fertilized chicken eggs. It’s a laborious process, closer to agriculture than it is high technology. Each batch incubates for nine to 12 days; the World Health Organization then spends months making the reagents manufacturers need to calibrate doses. The whole sequence runs about six months. That means that the flu strains in your vaccine in November were selected back in February. Which is a problem, because flu viruses don’t like to stand still. Between February and November, the virus drifts, and the current dominant H3N2 flu drifts especially fast . The eggs are a problem, too. Growing flu virus in a chicken egg forces it to adapt to egg cells, and those adaptations alter the very surface protein the vaccine is meant to teach your immune system to recognize. Between the 2011 and 2020 flu seasons, egg-adaptive mutations caused more mismatches than the virus’s own drift did. And more mismatches mean a less effective vaccine — while the flu shot prevented an estimated 12,000 deaths in the 2024–25 flu season, it is the weakest vaccine in routine American use, landing anywhere between 20 and 60 percent effective depending on how well February’s guess matched November’s virus. mRNA skips the egg. The shot carries instructions, a strip of genetic code that tells your own cells to build the flu’s surface protein, which your immune system then learns to attack. And swapping in a new strain means retyping that code, not growing a new virus. As a result, Moderna told the FDA’s advisory panel it can go from strain selection to finished vaccine in two to three months instead of six . That means strain picks could move later, closer to the season they cover, and a novel flu virus surfacing in September could still be blocked by a reformulated vaccine in the same season. Eggs are great, but they can’t do that. Back in January I wrote here about the universal flu vaccine — one shot covering every strain for years. It’s a public health dream. mFLUSIVA isn’t that, but some of the best hopes for a universal flu vaccine run through the mRNA platform, and platforms only improve when somebody uses them. That word — platform — is where last August’s decision went wrong. Kennedy made a claim about one application, mRNA respiratory vaccines, and cut funding for the technology underneath all of them . But over the 12 months that followed, the science on mRNA kept flowing. In June, five-year melanoma results showed an individualized mRNA therapy given after surgery alongside pembrolizumab cut the risk of recurrence or death by 49 percent . In April, a Memorial Sloan Kettering team reported that among pancreatic cancer patients whose immune systems responded to a personalized mRNA vaccine, nearly 90 percent were alive six years later ; the five-year survival rate in that disease sits near 13 percent. And KJ Muldoon, the first person treated with a gene-editing therapy built for his mutation alone , is walking and talking, though half the infants born with his disorder never see a first birthday. The editor that rewrote his DNA was delivered to his liver as messenger RNA — mRNA as the delivery truck rather than the vaccine. None of those is a flu shot. All of them are the same chemistry — a strip of genetic code wrapped in a lipid nanoparticle — and none of them were what Kennedy was talking about when he defunded it. Partially as a result, Americans are falling behind. Moderna’s combined Covid-and-flu shot is already licensed in Europe while patients here wait for a resubmission. The Phase 3 trial of its H5 bird flu vaccine — the one meant to be ready if bird flu ever learns to spread between people — runs on money from CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, and the British government , after the administration killed a $760 million BARDA contract. “The United States invented this platform,” Johns Hopkins RNA biologist Jeff Coller wrote on Thursday , “and is the only country walking away from it.” mFLUSIVA beat a standard-dose flu shot by 26.6 percent in a 40,700-person trial . (Against flu bad enough to send someone to a doctor, the figure was 33.7 percent — an exploratory finding the trial wasn’t built to prove, but that points in the same direction.) This is a better flu shot, but it hasn’t solved flu. There are issues with side effects: two-thirds of recipients reported injection-site pain, against 30 percent for the comparison. Most cleared in a day or two, but in a country where a quarter of the people who skip the flu shot cite side effects, that’s not a minor problem. And approval, unfortunately, isn’t access. The CDC’s vaccine advisory committee has been frozen by a federal court since March , so there is no clinical recommendation, which means insurers aren’t required to cover mFLUSIVA at no cost. The $500 million in canceled contracts hasn’t been restored. As Michael Osterholm, who runs the University of Minnesota’s infectious disease center, put it after the government reversed its mRNA decision in February: “We don’t have any idea why they reversed course. That’s part of the problem.” The most optimistic reading is that nine independent experts appointed by this government looked at the evidence on mRNA and could not produce a single vote against it . The more pessimistic one is that it took a refusal-to-file letter, a public outcry and two senior departures to get there. But here’s what we do know: Some morning this fall a 58-year-old will roll up a sleeve at a CVS for a vaccine designed off a sequence rather than grown in an egg, and will think about none of this. That’s more progress than I would have expected a year ago. A version of this story originally appeared in the Good News newsletter. Sign up here! ##段落
未来完美时态
流感疫苗为何如此难以改进的奇怪原因
美国终于有了mRNA流感疫苗。现在，真正的挑战是如何实际使用它。
作者：Bryan Walsh 2026年8月8日 12:00 PM UTC
赠送
Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe via Getty Images
Bryan Walsh是Vox的高级编辑总监，负责未来完美栏目及音视频内容中的人工智能等主题，并撰写《好消息》通讯。他曾在《时代》杂志工作15年，担任亚洲驻外记者、气候撰稿人和国际编辑，并著有一本关于生存风险的书。

##段落
2025年8月5日，美国卫生与公众服务部取消了22个mRNA疫苗项目，价值约5亿美元，并告知全国，将停止投资于这项曾为我们带来救命新冠疫苗的技术。卫生部长小罗伯特·F·肯尼迪，一位长期对疫苗持怀疑态度的人士，声称数据显示这些疫苗无法预防新冠和流感等上呼吸道感染。尽管他的说法并不属实——Moderna早已公布了显示相反结果的3期临床试验数据——但这似乎并不重要。

##段落

##段落
2026年8月5日——整整一年后——美国食品药品监督管理局（FDA）批准了mFLUSIVA，这是美国首个获得许可的mRNA流感疫苗。这种时间上的对称性，虽然对我这类总在寻找历史韵律的写作者极为有用，却并非刻意安排。批准恰好落在一周年纪念日，只是因为该机构在今年2月为自己设定的截止日期——当时它先是拒绝审查Moderna的申请，15天后又推翻了自己的决定。

##段落
这一决定并未引起太多媒体关注，部分原因在于季节性流感是美国民众很少认真对待的疾病——过去这个秋冬，只有不到50%的美国成年人接种了流感疫苗。但流感绝非儿戏：2024-25流感季造成了5100万例感染、71万例住院和4.5万例死亡。这比去年美国因车祸死亡的人数还要多。而且流感病毒的危害并不会随着退烧而结束。在确诊感染后的一周内，心脏病发作的风险约为正常水平的六倍。因此，更好的流感疫苗至关重要。

##段落
但更有趣的是，这一批准揭示了它诞生于怎样的一个年份。九位一致投票认为该疫苗收益大于风险的专家，恰恰是在那位反对mRNA技术的部长任内被任命的。在被要求审视证据时，这些专家没有投出一张反对票。

反对这一决定。这算不上彻底改变心意，但在公共卫生的艰难时刻，这值得我们寄予希望——因为流感可能只是这项技术的起点。如果你打过流感疫苗，请感谢一只鸡。自1940年代以来，美国人接种的每一剂流感疫苗都是在受精鸡蛋中培养出来的。这是一个费力耗时的过程，更像农业而非高科技。每批疫苗孵育9到12天；世界卫生组织随后花费数月时间制备制造商校准剂量所需的试剂。整个流程大约需要六个月。这意味着，你11月接种的疫苗中的流感毒株早在2月就已选定。这是个问题，因为流感病毒不会静止不动。从2月到11月，病毒会发生漂移，而当前主导的H3N2流感尤其漂移迅速。鸡蛋也是个问题。在鸡蛋中培养流感病毒会迫使它适应鸡胚细胞，而这些适应会改变疫苗本应教导你免疫系统识别的表面蛋白。在2011年至2020年的流感季节中，鸡胚适应性突变导致的错配比病毒自身漂移造成的错配更多。而更多错配意味着疫苗效果更差——尽管流感疫苗在2024-25流感季估计预防了12,000例死亡，但它仍是美国常规使用中效果最弱的疫苗，有效率在20%到60%之间，取决于2月的猜测与11月的病毒匹配程度。mRNA绕过了鸡蛋。疫苗携带指令，一段遗传代码，告诉你的细胞构建流感表面蛋白，你的免疫系统随后学会攻击它。而更换新毒株只需重新输入代码，无需培养新病毒。因此，Moderna向FDA咨询委员会表示，它可以将从毒株选择到成品疫苗的时间从六个月缩短到两到三个月。这意味着毒株选择可以推迟，更接近所覆盖的季节，而9月出现的新型流感病毒仍可能被同季重新配方的疫苗所阻断。鸡蛋很好，但做不到这一点。今年1月，我曾在此写过通用流感疫苗——一针覆盖所有毒株、效力持续数年。这是公共卫生的梦想。mFLUSIVA并非如此，但一些对通用流感疫苗的最大希望正寄托于mRNA平台，而平台只有被使用才能进步。“平台”这个词正是去年8月决定出错的地方。肯尼迪对mRNA呼吸道疫苗这一具体应用提出质疑，却削减了支撑所有这些应用的技术资金。但在随后的12个月里，mRNA科学持续向前。6月，五年黑色素瘤结果显示，术后单独给予的个体化mRNA疗法——

辅助使用pembrolizumab可将复发或死亡风险降低49%。今年4月，纪念斯隆凯特琳癌症中心的一个团队报告称，在免疫系统对个性化mRNA疫苗有反应的胰腺癌患者中，近90%在六年后仍然存活；而该疾病的五年生存率约为13%。KJ Muldoon是首个接受针对其独特突变设计的基因编辑疗法的人，他现在能行走、能说话，尽管患有他这种疾病的婴儿中有一半活不过一岁。改写他DNA的编辑器是以信使RNA形式递送到肝脏的——mRNA在这里是运输工具，而非疫苗。这些都不是流感疫苗。但它们都属于同一种化学原理——包裹在脂质纳米颗粒中的一段遗传密码——而肯尼迪在削减资金时，一个都没提到。部分结果是，美国人正在落后。Moderna的新冠流感联合疫苗已在欧洲获批，而美国患者还在等待重新提交申请。其H5禽流感疫苗的III期试验——旨在应对禽流感可能学会人际传播的情况——目前依赖流行病防范创新联盟（CEPI）和英国政府的资金，因为政府取消了价值7.6亿美元的BARDA合同。“美国发明了这个平台，”约翰斯·霍普金斯大学RNA生物学家Jeff Coller周四写道，“却也是唯一一个放弃它的国家。”在一项涉及40,700人的试验中，mFLUSIVA比标准剂量流感疫苗的有效性高出26.6%。（对于严重到需要就医的流感，这一数字为33.7%——这是一个探索性发现，试验并非为此设计，但指向相同方向。）这是一款更好的流感疫苗，但并未解决流感问题。副作用方面存在隐忧：三分之二接种者报告注射部位疼痛，而对照组为30%。大多数在一两天内缓解，但在一个有四分之一跳过流感疫苗的人声称是副作用所致国家，这不是小问题。而且，获批不等于可及。自3月以来，CDC的疫苗咨询委员会因联邦法院裁决而陷入僵局，因此没有临床建议，这意味着保险公司无需免费覆盖mFLUSIVA。被取消的5亿美元合同尚未恢复。正如明尼苏达大学传染病中心主任Michael Osterholm在政府2月逆转mRNA决定后所说：“我们完全不知道他们为何改变立场。这就是问题的一部分。”最乐观的看法是，政府任命的九位独立专家审视了mRNA的证据，没有一人投反对票；而更悲观的看法是……

走到这一步，靠的是一封拒绝受理函、公众的强烈抗议，以及两位高管的离职。但我们现在能确定的是：今年秋天某个早晨，一位58岁的人会在CVS卷起袖子，接种一剂基于基因序列设计而非在鸡蛋中培育的疫苗，而他对此毫不在意。这比我一年前预期的进展要大得多。这个故事的一个版本最初出现在《好消息》通讯中。点击此处订阅！查看更多：未来完美 好消息 健康 政治 公共卫生 特朗普政府 用最新的Vox填字游戏放松一下大脑 唐纳德·特朗普有个气体问题 播客 Ozempic仍然无法解决的一件事 流感疫苗为何如此难以改进的奇怪原因 我们忽视的世界末日威胁 播客 邮箱（必填） 订阅 提交您的邮箱即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。广告客户内容 来自 这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: There’s a know-it-all at every job — here’s how to deal
body: There’s a know-it-all at every job — here’s how to deal

Lucia dreaded interacting with her colleague Ray. Meetings that were scheduled for an hour would last two; once Ray started talking, he wouldn’t stop. “There’s no doubt he was a smart man,” Lucia says, “but he did little more than talk about everything he knew. He delegated almost all of his work to others.”

Most of us have dealt with a Ray, the know-it-all who is convinced they’re the smartest person in the room, hogs airtime in meetings  and has no qualms about interrupting others. They gleefully inform you of what’s right, even if they’re clearly wrong , lacking information or fail to understand the nuances of a situation.
Here are some of the signs of the know-it-all:
• Monopolizes conversations, refusing to be interrupted and talking over others
• Does not listen to or heed criticism or feedback
• Explains things that others already understand
• Rarely asks questions or displays curiosity
• Steals or doesn’t share credit for group successes

One reason know-it-alls exist in so many workplaces is that many organizations reward people who act as if they have all the answers. Do employees who state their ideas with conviction tend to get more support for those ideas at your job? If people appear uncertain, are they considered weak? In many cultures, decision-making is a competitive sport, rather than a collaborative effort, so acting like you know everything is a shrewd survival technique.
So how can you make your interactions with your know-it-all coworker not just less annoying but less damaging?
First, answer these four questions before taking action.
Question 1: Are they trying to prove something?

There’s a good chance your colleague’s egotism is compensating for some deficiency or fear. Considering their underlying insecurities may give you some clues about how to deal with them. For example, some know-it-alls might be constantly talking about what they accomplished in their last role as a way to demonstrate their value. If you understand that, you might make a point of validating the contributions they’re already making, freeing them from the need to tout their past achievements.
Question 2: Is their confidence warranted?

Your know-it-all colleague might have good reason to be confident in their assertions or claims, even if their demeanor leaves something to be desired. Could it be that their delivery is abrasive, but their underlying points have merit?
Question 3: Is bias playing a role in how I’m perceiving them?

We all hold biases about who is cut out to hold positions of power. And when someone doesn’t fit our preconceptions of leadership, we tend to question whether their confidence is justified. For example, research has shown that women of color have to prove their expertise over and over. Is the person you’re labeling as a know-it-all from an underestimated group? Do they belong to a culture or demographic that you have unconscious but negative biases about?
Question 4: Is their confidence pushing your buttons?

I admit that the stronger someone feels about something, the more I feel resistant to their argument, especially if their view threatens my values in some way. Ask yourself whether your reaction to your colleague has more to do with you than it does with them. Is it possible that you feel insecure when you compare your accomplishments to theirs? Or maybe you wish that you were as confident or sure minded as they are? Is their behavior causing real issues for you or the team? Or is it just annoying? Distinguish between statements or actions that are irritating and behavior that is preventing you from getting your work done.

After you can get a sense of where they’re coming from — and what role your preferences and biases may be playing in your attitude towards them — change your working relationship by trying one of these tactics.
Tactic 1: Appreciate what they have to offer

You may need to dig deep to find it, but there is probably some genuine knowledge or capability behind the know-it-all’s overconfidence. Sure, they may exaggerate their skills and successes but find the kernel of truth. And if the ultimate goal of their pretentiousness is approval or acceptance, your empathy and appreciation may help them let up on the “Look-how-much-I-know!” routine.

Most know-it-alls have an annoying habit of constantly interrupting people. One way to deal with it is to preemptively request that people refrain from interjecting. Before you start talking, explain how much time (roughly) you’re going to need and say something like, “Please hold any comments or questions until I’m done.” If you’re not making a formal presentation but are just having a discussion where some back-and-forth is expected, you might say instead, “Interruptions break my concentration, so I’d appreciate it if you’d let me finish my thoughts before jumping in.”
Tactic 3: When interruptions do occur, tactfully address them

If your efforts to preempt interruptions fail, address them directly. But don’t just raise your voice. That sets up a power struggle and your colleague is likely to talk louder in an attempt to drown you out. Instead, confidently say, “I’m going to finish my point, and then I’d love to hear what you have to say.”

If you don’t feel comfortable speaking up, enlist allies. It’s often easier for someone else to confront rudeness, saying something like, “I’d love to hear what Keith was saying before we move on,” or “I don’t think Madison was finished with her point.” If the know-it-all interrupts multiple people on your team, you could agree to speak up for each other when it happens.
One norm that I’ve been using when I’m teaching a workshop or giving a talk to a group where people will be interacting with one another (especially on Zoom) is to “take space, make space.”

The idea is that if you tend to be someone who stays quiet in meetings, you should challenge yourself to voice your opinions. If you’re someone who is prone to holding the floor, try to step back and make room for others to contribute. I’ve found that sharing this idea at the beginning results in a more equitably distributed meeting. This could be one of several norms you and your team agree on. Having established guidelines will discourage interruptions and make it safe for everyone to speak up.

Another irritating habit of the know-it-all is to proclaim: “Our customers expect us to deliver new features every six months.” “Sales are dropping because we aren’t quick enough to respond to complaints.” “In a year, no one will even be talking about this election.” If you’re sitting there wondering how they know that, it’s OK to ask for sources or data that back up their declarations.

每个工作场所都有个“万事通”——这样应对最有效  
2023年5月30日  
/  
艾米·加洛  
Facebook  
X  
LinkedIn  
Reddit  
WhatsApp  
文辉·郑  
露西亚害怕与同事雷打交道。原定一小时的会议会拖到两小时；一旦雷开始说话，他就停不下来。“毫无疑问他是个聪明人，”露西亚说，“但他几乎只谈论自己知道的一切。他把几乎所有工作都委派给了别人。”  
我们大多数人都遇到过像雷这样的人，这种“万事通”坚信自己是房间里最聪明的人，在会议上霸占发言时间，并且毫无顾忌地打断别人。他们兴高采烈地告诉你什么是对的，即使他们显然错了、缺乏信息或未能理解情况的细微差别。  
以下是“万事通”的一些特征：  
• 垄断对话，拒绝被打断，并压过他人发言  
• 不听或不理会批评或反馈  
• 用居高临下的语气说话  
• 解释别人已经理解的事情  
• 很少提问或表现出好奇心  
• 抢占或不分享团队成功的功劳  
“万事通”在如此多工作场所存在的一个原因是，许多组织会奖励那些表现得好像拥有所有答案的人。在你的工作中，那些坚定表达自己观点的员工是否更容易获得支持？如果人们显得不确定，他们是否被视为软弱？在许多文化中，决策是一场竞争性运动，而非协作努力，因此表现得好像你什么都知道是一种精明的生存技巧。  
那么，你如何让与“万事通”同事的互动不仅不那么令人恼火，而且不那么有害呢？  
首先，在采取行动之前回答这四个问题。  
问题1：他们是在试图证明什么吗？  
你的同事的自大很可能是在弥补某种缺陷或恐惧。考虑他们潜在的不安全感可能会给你一些应对他们的线索。例如，一些“万事通”可能会不断谈论他们在上一份工作中取得的成就，以此展示自己的价值。如果你理解了这一点，你可能会特意肯定他们目前所做的贡献，让他们不再需要炫耀过去的成就。  
问题2：他们的自信是否有依据？  
你的“万事通”同事可能完全有理由对自己的断言或主张充满信心，即使他们的态度有些欠缺。会不会是他们的表达方式令人不快，但他们的核心观点其实有道理？  
问题3：偏见是否影响了我对他们的看法？  
我们所有人都对谁适合担任权力职位抱有偏见。当某人不符合我们对领导者的先入为主的观念时，

在探讨领导力时，我们往往会质疑他们的自信是否名副其实。例如，研究表明，有色人种女性不得不反复证明自己的专业能力。你贴上“万事通”标签的那个人，是否来自一个被低估的群体？他们是否属于你在潜意识中抱有负面偏见的某种文化或人群？

问题四：他们的自信是否触动了你的敏感神经？

我承认，一个人对某件事的态度越强硬，我就越容易对其论点产生抵触，尤其是当他们的观点在某种程度上威胁到我的价值观时。问问自己，你对同事的反应是否更多与自身有关，而非他们本身。当你将自己的成就与他们的相比时，是否会感到不安？或者你希望自己能像他们一样自信或坚定？他们的行为是否真的给你或团队带来了实际问题，还是仅仅令人不快？区分那些令人恼火的言论或行动与阻碍你完成工作的行为。

当你能够理解他们的出发点——以及你的偏好和偏见在影响你对他们的态度中扮演了什么角色——尝试通过以下策略之一来改变你们的工作关系。

策略一：欣赏他们所能提供的价值

你可能需要深入挖掘才能发现，但在“万事通”的过度自信背后，很可能存在某种真正的知识或能力。当然，他们可能夸大自己的技能和成功，但请找到其中的真实核心。如果他们装腔作势的最终目的是获得认可或接纳，你的同理心和欣赏或许能帮助他们放松“看我懂多少！”的表演套路。

策略二：防止打断

大多数“万事通”都有不断打断别人的恼人习惯。一种应对方法是预先请求人们避免插话。在开始发言前，说明你大概需要多长时间，并说类似“请在我讲完之前不要发表评论或提问”的话。如果你不是在做正式演示，而只是进行预期会有来回交流的讨论，你可以改为说：“打断会分散我的注意力，所以如果你能让我把想法说完再插话，我会很感激。”

策略三：当打断确实发生时，得体地应对

如果你预防打断的努力失败了，就直接面对。但不要只是提高音量，那会引发权力斗争，而你的同事可能会更大声地试图盖过你。相反，自信地说：“我会先说完我的观点，然后我很乐意听听你要说什么。”

如果你觉得直接开口不舒服，可以寻求盟友。通常，让别人去面对粗鲁行为会更容易，比如这样说：

##段落
比如，“我很想听听基思在我们继续之前说了什么”，或者“我觉得麦迪逊还没说完她的观点”。如果“万事通”多次打断你团队里其他人的发言，你们可以约定好，在发生这种情况时互相帮忙发声。

##段落
策略四：设定规则
我在主持研讨会或与需要互动的人群（尤其是在Zoom上）讲话时，一直使用的一个规则是“争取空间，留出空间”。
这个理念是，如果你倾向于在会议上保持沉默，就应该挑战自己说出想法。如果你容易占据话语主导权，试着退一步，为他人创造贡献的机会。我发现，在开始时分享这个想法，会让会议发言更均衡。这可以是你和团队商定的多项规则之一。有了明确的指导方针，就能减少打断，让大家都能安心发言。

##段落
策略五：要求事实和数据
“万事通”另一个令人恼火的习惯是宣称：“我们的客户期望我们每六个月推出新功能。”“销售下滑是因为我们对投诉响应不够快。”“一年之内，没人会再谈论这场选举。”如果你坐在那里纳闷他们怎么知道的，完全可以要求他们提供支持这些说法的来源或数据。
这样做时要保持尊重，不要对抗。你可以说类似“我不确定我们基于的假设和事实是否一致。让我们退一步，先看看数据再做决定。”
即使你那位专横的同事前几次对这些质询反应不佳，他们也可能逐渐习惯你要求证据，并在脱口而出未经证实的论断前三思。而要求他们解释自己如何知道某事，或许能帮他们认识到自身知识的局限，将来更谦逊一些。
当你与“万事通”开会时，要带着已核实的事实出席。你越准备充分，越能捍卫自己的观点并反驳他们的误导性陈述，效果就越好。你也在强化基于事实的讨论而非装腔作势的重要性。

##段落
策略六：展现谦逊与开放心态
许多爱炫耀的人之所以如此行事，是因为这在过去行之有效，或者因为他们或明或暗地收到过信息——展现自信是团队、组织或他们所处文化所期望的。你可以通过展现谦逊和开放心态来提供另一种榜样。试着说“我不知道”或“我现在没有这个信息，回头告诉你”。
如果“万事通”看到你表达不确定并不会带来什么后果，他们可能就会明白，承认自己不知道是完全可以接受的。

他们可能也愿意这样做。你甚至可以鼓励每个人在参加会议前，就他们想提出的解决方案或想法，事先思考其利弊，从而促使他们更加谦逊。或者，你可以提出这样的问题：
• 还有别的观点吗？
• 如果我们尝试从另一个角度看这个问题，我们会怎么想？
• 这种方法的优点和风险是什么？

因为有些自以为是的人是在寻求认可，简单地肯定他们的想法就能防止他们夸夸其谈。在分享你的观点或提出问题之前，感谢他们分享想法，或者强调你欣赏他们观点的两个点。例如，你可以说：“这是个有用的观点。我同意你所说的第一部分，对第二部分我略有不同看法。我们来讨论一下。”

与自以为是的人共事，轻则令人恼火，重则阻碍职业发展。但你无需坐视不理，默默忍受。你可以采取措施来抑制同事的虚张声势，或至少减轻其对你和他人的影响。

readings.title: The doomsday threat we’re ignoring
body: Future Perfect The doomsday threat we’re ignoring The writer Annie Jacobsen on the terrifying realities of biological war. by Avishay Artsy and Noel King Aug 9, 2026, 11:00 AM UTC Gift Jahi Chikwendiu/The Washington Post via Getty Images Of all the extinction-level threats vying for our attention, AI, climate change, and nuclear war tend to get most of the airplay. But Annie Jacobsen thinks biological war should be near the top of our mental list of doomsday scenarios, too. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. She should know — Jacobsen has carved out a unique niche as America’s foremost reporter on the ways we could end the world. Her bestselling 2024 book Nuclear War: A Scenario terrified readers and experts alike, and has been optioned by Hollywood. It was while conducting dozens of interviews with high-level government sources for Nuclear War that Jacobsen was told repeatedly that biowarfare should be her next focus. She took their advice. Her gripping new book Biological War: A Scenario follows a similar ticking-clock format that shows, step by step, just how a humanity-threatening man-made biological catastrophe could play out. (Spoiler alert: not great.) The result feels like dystopian science fiction, albeit the kind that comes heavily footnoted with government studies that come to similarly grim conclusions. The fact that tech CEOs are also sounding the alarm that advanced AI could make creating killer germs even easier only adds to the growing sense of anxiety. And this book has also been optioned by Hollywood for a TV adaptation. Jacobsen sat down with Today, Explained host Noel King to talk through the plot of her nightmare scenario, why we’re still developing biological weapons despite the clear risks, and what needs to happen to avoid disaster. Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .

How does your book start? The inciting incident in the book is an accident at a Biosafety Level 4 lab, shorthand BSL-4, in Siberia called Vector. And it’s an actual BSL-4 lab, the highest classification. ... And there was an actual accident, an explosion there in 2019 . In that real-life incident, a deadly pathogen was not released that we know of. But of course, in Biological War: A Scenario , a deadly pathogen is released. And it’s a form of pneumonic plague, which is a nightmare pathogen and sits at the top of the Tier 1 select agent list of the CDC . And so in the first act of the book, I show the scrambling of the intelligence community and the Defense Department, trying desperately to determine if something got out and what it is. ... The release of the pathogen widens, and so once you have escape. You do not have mitigation, which has to happen in the first 24, 48 hours. Now you have a situation which is unstoppable. You say this is now an unstoppable scenario. What is it? A plague itself, of course, conjures up images and ideas of the bubonic plague of the 14th century, the Black Death. That killed between one half and one third of Europe . The bacteria is called Yersinia pestis. And pneumonic plague is the airborne version of plague. The problem with an airborne pathogen is that because the delivery system is the human lungs, it can move very quickly from a scientist in that lab who now has Yersinia pestis in his lungs out to the general public. And that is precisely what happens in the scenario. How does it spread from there? The city where this BSL-4 lab sits isn’t Moscow. What happens once the pathogen is in the lungs of the people who work in that lab, or the janitor who was cleaning it that night? That’s right. Well, suddenly it’s in everyone’s lungs, and those people go out into their community. And even though Koltsovo, the science town where Vector is located, is a small town, it is just 12 miles from Novosibirsk, which is the third-largest city in Russia. And, also, there happens to be in this scenario a group of international hunters on a hunting trip in that area who come across a dying scientist in the snow. One of them gives him CPR, being the Good Samaritan that he is. And lo and behold, those travelers suddenly are now getting on an airplane in Novosibirsk, flying home to where they reside in five or six of the continents. What makes this form of plague so novel, so dangerous? I pull this information from actual facts of the Soviet Cold War-era biological weapons program that we know about from Soviet defectors. And I want you to keep in mind: This is 40 years ago when gene editing was in its infancy. But there are two things specifically that the Soviet bioweapons engineers did to plague. Their idea was to create a super plague weapon. And one of them has never been revealed before. They were working to insert the gene for euphoria into the plague pathogen. ... When you get a disease, a pneumonic-type disease, pneumonia, tubercular, you want to go home and get under the covers because you feel terrible. And when you do that, you’re infecting a lot less people than you would if a gene for euphoria had been inserted into the pathogen, which would make you feel terrific, which would make you want to go out and socialize with people, perhaps even go to a crowded disco. And the other thing that the Soviet scientists were working on was a way to defeat medical countermeasures, but with an added component of psychological distress. They inserted a gene into the pathogen that would be triggered by the taking of antibiotics. And that second pathogen would give you encephalitis, which is a swelling of the brain. The psychological part of it, according to the Soviet scientists, was that they wanted the last thought of the person dying of what they thought was pneumonic plague, but would in fact be encephalitist to be, “My government and Western medicine has failed me.” Those of us who try to remain optimistic think there’s a way to stop it. In the movies, there’s an outbreak, then the government gets it under control, and okay, maybe a lot of people die, but we’re all right. That is not where your book is headed. How does your scenario end? So in the book, I take readers from outbreak to anarchy in six days. Anarchy is what will happen according to Pentagon war gaming and pandemic planning. And this is because fear of infection becomes a secondary weapon, if you will. People begin to behave like they are about to die, which is most certainly underpinning everyone’s mind. And so after those first six days, the Principals Committee, the President’s Biodefense Committee, must make a decision. The president has to declare the Insurrection Act, which allows the military to step in as a law enforcement agency. “Imagine the president — with a few Secret Service outside the door, the military aide with the nuclear football — sitting alone in a room wearing a gas mask.” What happens to the president really blew my mind as a reporter. He goes somewhere in the United States very far away from everyone. Because the idea, the goal, is to make sure that the president doesn’t get the airborne pathogen in his lungs. So maybe I’ll leave you with an image. Imagine the president — with a few Secret Service outside the door, the military aide with the nuclear football — sitting alone in a room wearing a gas mask. In the book, the people who survive are the ones who have gas masks. Everyone else is gone. And look, we hope we never get to that, by all means. But yes, the Pentagon has issued 1.7 million gas masks to its military personnel. And that is a spooky thought in and of itself, coupled with the idea that the military is predominantly male. There’s something like 17 percent women in the military. And so, unlike the Nuclear War scenario in which I had science-based nuclear winter theory to work from, in Biological War , nothing has been written on the science record about what it might be after. And so the one imaginative part of the book is the very end where I write about biological twilight. ... And it is a very, very ugly world. Let’s back up. We did outlaw biological weapons at some point, right? That’s right. Very mysteriously in 1969, President Nixon just unilaterally declared that the arsenal was going to be destroyed . At the same time that all of the nations of the world were working to sign this treaty called the Biological Weapons Convention Treaty, which would outlaw bioweapons. Soviet Russia at the time signed it but immediately began work on an illegal biological weapons program that was colossal. And this went without notice, without any idea really by the CIA and the Pentagon all the way until 1989, when one of the Soviet scientists named Vladimir Pasechnik had a crisis of conscience and he defected and he told British intelligence all about the program. Where have we seen biological weapons used? Maybe the most important example of a biological attack in the past, certainly here in the United States, are the anthrax attacks, which occurred right after 9/11. Weaponized anthrax was sent through the mail to US senators and a number of media outlets. So five people ended up dying; 22 got sick in four states. But that really kicked off what can be considered the biological military-industrial complex, if you will, which led to this buildup in BSL-4 labs around the world today. There are 110 BSL-4 labs around the world . There are more than 3,500 BSL-3 labs . Your book has a map of where those labs are, which I found weirdly comforting, mainly because I don’t live too near any of them. If one of these things is going to be released, either accidentally or deliberately, where is the threat coming from? A rogue nation? Terrorists? Certainly, bad actors getting a hold of a biological weapon was the great concern of the post-anthrax situation. And that is why so much emphasis was put on bioterrorism. Now I avoided that specifically in the book. ... And I didn’t even have an attack. Rather, I had an incident. I had a lab leak because I have learned in the decades since that really is the greatest concern. So many of these BSL-3 and 4 labs are in places without a lot of security, including in countries where there are wars going on. Could somebody be making a biological weapon in a basement somewhere, off books? Absolutely. And another disturbing document I came across, unclassified in the Pentagon, was a threat spectrum that showed weapons of mass destruction in terms of destructiveness. And of course, nuclear weapons sit at the far end of the spectrum. They are the most destructive. But very close behind were biological weapons. And even more startling was the notion that biological weapons present the greatest overall threat. Nuclear weapons have an extremely high barrier for entry. You have to have fissile material. ... You have to have a weapons delivery system like an ICBM or a submarine. ... That creates a situation where most nuclear weapons, all nuclear weapons, if you will, are in the hands of a command-and-control system within a nation. Biological weapons have no such barriers. In fact, the barriers for entry are getting lower literally by the day. You now can have a situation where someone with very limited knowledge of biology can create a biological weapon in their basement with the use of computational systems like an AI system, for example. Your book reads like a thriller. How much have you exaggerated? How much have you novelized in order to hold our attention? Everything in the book is based in science fact, meaning all of the facts, all of the figures. I write a hundred or so pages of notes in the back of the book for readers to be able to answer the question that you are asking me. ... In the notes, you can find that answer. Did any of those people give you good recommendations for how to avoid a disaster scenario, or at least how to avoid these things proliferating? Well, you know, the ticking clock scenario that I write has an even more urgent ticking clock, which is the public’s pressure on lawmakers to absolutely do something about this nightmare scenario before it happens. Look, we have a world right now where you have the CEOs of the largest AI companies in the world admitting publicly that the lane of bio mixed with AI is of their top concern. You don’t hear that about nuclear. You hear that about bio. How do you sleep through the night? Anyone who knows me personally can vouch for the fact that I am an optimist at heart. I really believe that information is king. Once you know things, it gives you a lot of power. Perhaps that’s whistling by the graveyard, but that’s what works for me. Do you have a biohazard suit? I do not. I do not. But I do have a few gas masks. I must tell the truth. See More : Future Perfect Health Podcasts Politics Public Health Today, Explained podcast World Politics Take a mental break with the newest Vox crossword Donald Trump has a gas problem Podcast The one thing Ozempic still can’t fix The strange reason flu shots have been so hard to improve The doomsday threat we’re ignoring Podcast Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . ##段落
未来完成时：我们忽视的末日威胁  
作家安妮·雅各布森谈生物战的可怕现实。  
作者：阿维沙伊·阿尔西与诺埃尔·金  
2026年8月9日，上午11:00 UTC  
赠阅  
贾希·奇肯迪乌/《华盛顿邮报》 via Getty Images  
在所有争夺我们注意力的灭绝级威胁中，人工智能、气候变化和核战争往往占据最多头条。但安妮·雅各布森认为，生物战也应排在我们末日情景心智清单的前列。

##段落
邮箱（必填）  
注册  
提交邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款与隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。  
她理应了解——雅各布森已开辟出一片独特领域，成为美国首屈一指的报道“人类可能如何终结世界”的记者。她2024年的畅销书《核战争：一种情景》令读者和专家 alike 胆寒，并已被好莱坞购得改编权。正是在为《核战争》采访数十位政府高层消息来源的过程中，雅各布森反复被告知，生物战应是她的下一个关注重点。她采纳了这些建议。

##段落
她的新书《生物战：一种情景》扣人心弦，采用类似的倒计时叙事格式，一步步展示一场威胁人类的人造生物灾难可能如何展开。（剧透警告：结果不妙。）读来宛如反乌托邦科幻小说，尽管是那种附有大量政府研究脚注、得出同样严峻结论的类型。科技公司CEO们也在敲响警钟，称先进人工智能可能让制造致命病原体变得更加容易，这只会加剧日益增长的焦虑感。这本书同样已被好莱坞购得改编权，计划拍成电视剧。

##段落
雅各布森与《今日解读》主持人诺埃尔·金坐下来，讨论了书中的噩梦情景情节、为什么我们明知风险巨大却仍在开发生物武器，以及需要采取什么措施才能避免灾难。以下是他们对话的节选，为篇幅和清晰度做了编辑。完整播客内容更丰富，欢迎在任何获取播客的平台收听《今日解读》，包括Apple Podcasts、Pandora和Spotify。

##段落
你的书是如何开篇的？  
书中的触发事件是西伯利亚一家名为Vector的生物安全四级实验室（简称BSL-4）发生的事故。这是一座真实的BSL-4实验室，属于最高安全等级……2019年那里确实发生过一次爆炸事故。在真实事件中，据我们所知没有致命病原体泄漏。但当然，在《生物战：一种情景》中，致命病原体被释放了。它是一种肺鼠疫变体，堪称噩梦级病原体，位列美国疾控中心一级选择病原体清单之首。因此，在书的第一幕中，我展示了情报部门的紧急应对……

该社区与国防部紧密合作，拼命试图确定是否有东西泄漏，以及泄漏的究竟是什么。……病原体的释放范围不断扩大，因此一旦发生泄漏，你就无法遏制，而遏制措施必须在最初的24到48小时内实施。如今，你面对的是一种无法阻挡的局面。你说，这现在成了一个不可阻挡的情景。它是什么呢？瘟疫本身，当然会让人联想到14世纪腺鼠疫和黑死病的景象和概念。那场瘟疫夺去了欧洲三分之一到一半的人口。这种细菌被称为鼠疫耶尔森菌。而肺鼠疫则是鼠疫的空气传播版本。空气传播病原体的问题在于，因为其传播系统是人类肺部，它可以从实验室中那位现在肺部带有鼠疫耶尔森菌的科学家迅速传播到公众中。而在这个情景中，这正是发生的事情。它如何从那里扩散？这个BSL-4实验室所在的城市不是莫斯科。一旦病原体进入实验室工作人员或当晚清洁工的肺部，会发生什么？没错，突然间它进入了每个人的肺里，而这些人走出社区。尽管科利佐沃——Vector所在的科学城——是一个小镇，但距离俄罗斯第三大城市新西伯利亚只有12英里。此外，在这个情景中，碰巧有一群国际猎人在该地区狩猎，他们在雪地里遇到一位垂死的科学家。其中一人出于善意，给他做了心肺复苏。果然，这些旅行者突然登上新西伯利亚的飞机，飞回他们在五大洲或六大洲的家。是什么让这种瘟疫形式如此新颖、如此危险？我从我们知道的苏联冷战时期生物武器计划的实际事实中提取这些信息，这些事实来自苏联叛逃者。我想让你记住：这是40年前，基因编辑还处于起步阶段。但苏联生物武器工程师对瘟疫做了两件特别的事情。他们的想法是制造一种超级瘟疫武器。其中一件从未被揭露过。他们试图将欣快感基因插入瘟疫病原体。……当你患上疾病，如肺型疾病、肺炎、结核病时，你想回家躲进被窝，因为你感觉非常糟糕。当你这样做时，你传染的人会少得多，而如果病原体被插入欣快感基因，你会感觉极好，会想出去与人交往，甚至可能去拥挤的迪斯科舞厅。苏联科学家研究的另一件事是击败我

##段落
除了标准的医疗对策外，还加入了心理折磨的成分。他们在病原体中插入了一个基因，该基因会在服用抗生素时被触发。而第二种病原体会让你患上脑炎，即大脑肿胀。据苏联科学家称，心理层面的设计是，他们希望一个以为自己死于肺鼠疫、但实际上死于脑炎的人，最后的念头是：“我的政府和西方医学辜负了我。”

##段落
我们中那些试图保持乐观的人认为，有办法阻止这一切。在电影里，疫情爆发，然后政府控制住局面，好吧，也许很多人死了，但我们没事。那不是你的书所指向的方向。你的设想结局如何？在书中，我带着读者从疫情爆发到无政府状态，只用了六天。无政府状态是五角大楼的战争推演和流行病规划所预测的结果。这是因为对感染的恐惧成了一种次级武器，或者说某种意义上的辅助武器。人们开始表现得像即将死去一样，这无疑笼罩在每个人的心头。

##段落
因此，在那最初的六天之后，总统的生物防御委员会——即“主要委员会”——必须做出决定。总统必须宣布《叛乱法》，允许军队作为执法机构介入。作为记者，总统的遭遇真的让我震惊。他去了美国某个远离所有人的地方。因为其理念和目标，是确保总统不会吸入空气中的病原体。

##段落
所以，也许我留给你一个画面。想象一下总统——门外站着几名特勤局特工，军事助理拎着核按钮手提箱——独自坐在一个房间里，戴着防毒面具。在书中，存活下来的人就是那些有防毒面具的人。其他人都不在了。当然，我们希望永远不要走到那一步。但确实，五角大楼已经向其军事人员发放了170万副防毒面具。这本身就令人不寒而栗，再加上军队以男性为主的事实——军队中女性大约只占17%。因此，与核战争设想中我可以基于科学的核冬天理论来推演不同，在生物战设想中，科学记录上没有任何关于其后可能发生什么的记载。所以，这本书中富有想象力的部分就是结尾，我写到了“生物黄昏”……那是一个非常、非常丑陋的世界。

##段落
让我们退一步看。我们确实在某个时候禁止了生物武器，对吧？没错。非常。

1969年，尼克松总统神秘地单方面宣布，美国的生物武器库将被销毁。与此同时，世界各国正在努力签署一项名为《生物武器公约》的条约，该条约将禁止生物武器。当时的苏联签署了该条约，但立即开始了一项规模庞大的非法生物武器计划。这一情况一直未被察觉，中央情报局和五角大楼对此毫无所知，直到1989年，一位名叫弗拉基米尔·帕塞奇尼克的苏联科学家因良心不安而叛逃，他向英国情报部门透露了整个计划。我们在哪里见过生物武器的使用？也许过去生物攻击最重要的例子，尤其是在美国，是炭疽袭击事件，发生在9/11事件后不久。武器化的炭疽通过邮件发送给美国参议员和多家媒体机构。结果导致五人死亡，四个州有22人患病。但这确实引发了所谓的生物军工复合体，如果可以用这个词的话，这导致了今天世界各地BSL-4实验室的扩张。全球有110个BSL-4实验室，还有超过3500个BSL-3实验室。你的书中有一张这些实验室位置的地图，我觉得这莫名令人安心，主要是因为我住的地方离它们都不太近。如果这些东西中的某一个被释放，无论是意外还是蓄意的，威胁来自哪里？流氓国家？恐怖分子？当然，坏分子获取生物武器是炭疽事件后最大的担忧。这就是为什么如此多的重点放在生物恐怖主义上。在书中我特意避开了这一点……我甚至没有涉及攻击事件。相反，我描述了一个事故。我提到了实验室泄漏，因为我在之后的几十年里学到，那才是最大的担忧。这么多BSL-3和4实验室位于缺乏安全保障的地方，包括一些正在发生战争的国家。有人可能在地下室秘密制造生物武器吗？绝对有可能。我遇到的另一份令人不安的文件，是五角大楼里一份未保密的文件，它展示了一个威胁谱系，按破坏力排列大规模杀伤性武器。当然，核武器位于谱系的远端，它们是最具破坏力的。但紧随其后的是生物武器。更令人震惊的是，生物武器构成了最大的整体威胁。核武器有极高的进入门槛。你必须拥有裂变材料……你必须拥有像洲际弹道导弹或潜艇这样的武器运载系统……这造成了一种局面，大多数核武器，所有核武

##段落
如果说武器掌握在国家指挥控制体系手中，生物武器则毫无此类屏障。事实上，进入门槛正逐日降低。如今，一个对生物学了解甚少的人，借助人工智能等计算系统，就能在自家地下室制造生物武器。你的书读起来像惊悚小说。你在多大程度上进行了夸张？为了吸引读者，你又虚构了多少内容？书中一切皆基于科学事实，所有数据、所有数字皆属实。我在书末写了上百页注释，让读者能够回答你刚才提出的问题……在注释中，你能找到答案。那些受访者是否给出了好的建议，教我们如何避免灾难情景，或至少防止这些威胁扩散？你知道，我写的“倒计时”情景背后还有一个更紧迫的倒计时——那就是公众向立法者施压，要求他们在噩梦发生前采取绝对行动。看看当下世界，全球最大AI公司的CEO们公开承认，生物与AI结合的领域是他们最担忧的问题之一。你不会听到他们这样谈论核武器，但你会听到他们这样谈论生物。你晚上怎么睡得着？任何了解我的人都能作证，我骨子里是个乐观主义者。我真心相信信息为王。一旦你了解事物，你就拥有了巨大力量。也许这不过是走过墓地时吹口哨壮胆，但对我行之有效。你有生物危害防护服吗？我没有。真没有。但我确实有几副防毒面具。我必须说实话。查看更多：Future Perfect Health Podcasts Politics Public Health Today, Explained podcast World Politics 用最新的Vox填字游戏放松一下大脑 唐纳德·特朗普有个气体问题 播客 Ozempic仍无法解决的唯一一件事 流感疫苗为何如此难以改进的奇怪原因 我们正在忽视的世界末日威胁 播客 邮箱（必填） 订阅 提交邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。广告客户内容 这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
body: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
We persist in hiring and training as if we’re running a bowling squad, as if easily measured skills are all that matter.

What causes successful organizations to fail ? What makes stocks fade, innovations slow, customers jump ship? We can agree that certain skills are essential. That hiring coders who can’t code, salespeople who can’t sell, or architects who can’t design is a waste. But these skills — let’s call them vocational skills — have become the backbone of the recruitment process.

But how do you explain that similar organizations, with similarly vocationally skilled people, find themselves with very different outcomes? Most of the textbooks that students experience and the tests they take are about vocational skills, the checkboxes that have to be checked to get a job. By misdefining “vocational” and focusing on these allegedly essential skills, we’ve diminished the value of the other skills that matter.

We give too little respect to the other skills when we call them “soft” and imply that they’re optional. What actually separates thriving organizations from struggling ones are the difficult-to-measure attitudes, processes and perceptions of the people who do the work.

Vocational skills can be taught: You’re not born knowing engineering or copywriting or even graphic design, therefore they must be something we can teach. But we let ourselves off the hook when it comes to decision-making, eager participation, dancing with fear, speaking with authority, working in teams , seeing the truth, speaking the truth, inspiring others, doing more than we’re asked, caring and being willing to change things. We underinvest in this training, fearful that these things are innate and can’t be taught. Perhaps they’re talents. And so we downplay them, calling them soft skills, making it easy for us to move on to something seemingly more urgent.

At scale, organizations pay less attention to soft skills when hiring because we’ve persuaded ourselves that vocational skills are impersonal and easier to measure. If it’s easier to test for, it seems more important when selecting our team.
And we fire slowly (and retrain rarely) when these skills are missing, because we’re worried about stepping on toes, being called out for getting personal or possibly wasting time on a lost cause.

But these skills can all be learned, as obvious skills like chess or typing can be learned. We learn them accidentally, by osmosis, by the collisions we have with teachers, parents, bosses and the world. Even though they’re more difficult to measure, that doesn’t mean we can’t improve them, can’t practice them or can’t change the way we do our work.

Let’s stop calling them soft. They’re interpersonal skills. Leadership skills. The skills of charisma and diligence and contribution. But these modifiers, while accurate, somehow edge them away from the vocational skills, the skills that we actually hire for, the skills we measure a graduate degree on.
So let’s uncomfortably call them real skills instead.
Real because they work, because they’re at the heart of what we need today.
Real because even if you’ve got the vocational skills, you’re no help to us without these human skills, the things that we can’t write down or program a computer to do.
Real skills can’t replace vocational skills, of course. What they can do is amplify the things you’ve already been measuring.
Imagine a team member with all the traditional vocational skills: productive, skilled, experienced. A resume that can prove it. That’s a fine baseline.

Now add to it. Perceptive, charismatic, driven, focused, goal-setting, inspiring and motivated. Generous, empathic and consistent. A deep listener , with patience. What happens to your organization when someone like that joins your team?
Writing in the Harvard Business Review , Lou Solomon reports that 69 percent of managers are uncomfortable communicating with their employees. I’d guess that many of the other 31 percent are lying.

Communicating with employees is uncomfortable because we’ve built systems of compliance and dominance that make it difficult. We ask people to leave their humanity at the door, then use authority to change behavior. We overlay corporate greed and short-term thinking with a human desire to create work that matters.

How do we build people-centric organizations while also accepting the fact that two thirds of our managers (presumably well paid, well trained and integral to our success) are so uncomfortable doing an essential part of their job that they admitted it to a stranger?

In a recent survey, the Graduate Management Admission Council reported that although MBAs were strong in analytical aptitude, quantitative expertise and information-gathering ability, they were sorely lacking in other critical areas that employers find equally attractive: strategic thinking, written and oral communication, leadership and adaptability . Are these mutually exclusive? Must we trade one for the other?

The foundation of all real skills is this one: the confidence and permission to talk to one another. Not to manage, belittle, intimidate or control. Simply to seek to be understood and to do the work to understand.

Excerpted from The Song of Significance: A New Manifesto for Teams by Seth Godin, in agreement with Portfolio, an imprint of Penguin Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House LLC. Copyright © Seth Godin 2023.

He is the founder of the altMBA, the social media pioneer Squidoo, and Yoyodyne, one of the first internet companies. Find out more at seths.blog.

##段落
让我们停止称它们为“软技能”——改称“真实技能”吧  
2023年6月9日  
/  
赛斯·戈丁  
Facebook  
X  
LinkedIn  
Reddit  
WhatsApp  
黛博拉·斯皮尔曼  

##段落
我们坚持像运营保龄球队一样进行招聘和培训，仿佛只有易于衡量的技能才重要。

##段落
是什么导致成功组织走向失败？是什么让股价黯淡、创新放缓、客户流失？我们都能认同某些技能至关重要。雇佣不会写代码的程序员、不会销售的销售员、或不会设计的建筑师，纯属浪费。但这些技能——我们姑且称之为职业技能——已成为招聘流程的支柱。

##段落
但如何解释那些拥有相似职业技能人才、结构类似的机构，最终却走向截然不同的结局？学生接触的大多数教科书和参加的考试，都围绕职业技能展开，即为了获得工作必须打勾的那些选项。由于错误定义“职业性”，并过分聚焦于这些所谓的关键技能，我们贬低了其他真正重要技能的价值。

##段落
当我们称其他技能为“软”技能，暗示它们是可有可无时，我们给予的尊重实在太少。真正区分蓬勃发展组织与挣扎求生组织的，是那些难以衡量的态度、流程以及从业者的认知。

##段落
职业技能可以传授：你并非天生就懂工程、文案甚至平面设计，因此它们必定是可教的。但在决策、积极参与、与恐惧共舞、权威表达、团队协作、洞察真相、直言不讳、激励他人、超越要求、关怀他人以及勇于改变这些事情上，我们却让自己轻易脱身。我们对这类培训投入不足，担心这些能力是与生俱来、无法教授的。或许它们是天赋。于是我们淡化它们，称其为软技能，好让我们轻松转向看似更紧迫的事务。

##段落
在规模化运营中，组织在招聘时对软技能的关注较少，因为我们说服自己，职业技能是非个人化的、更容易衡量。如果某项技能更容易测试，在选拔团队时它就显得更重要。

##段落
而当这些软技能缺失时，我们却迟迟不解雇（也很少再培训），因为我们担心得罪人、担心被指责针对个人，或担心在无可救药的事情上浪费时间。

##段落
但这些技能全部可以学习，就像下棋或打字这类显而易见的技能一样可以习得。我们通过偶然经历、耳濡目染、以及与老师、父母、老板和世界的碰撞来学习它们。尽管它们更难衡量，但这并不意味着我们无法提升它们、无法练习它们。

##段落
我们无法改变，或者无法改变我们的工作方式。
当然可以。
让我们别再称它们为“软技能”了。它们是人际技能，领导技能，是魅力、勤奋和贡献的技能。但这些修饰词，虽然准确，却不知怎地让它们偏离了职业技能——那些我们真正为之招聘的技能，那些我们用来衡量学位的技能。
所以，让我们不自在地称它们为“真实技能”吧。
真实，因为它们行之有效，因为它们是我们今天所需的核心。
真实，因为即使你拥有职业技能，没有这些人性技能——那些我们无法写下来或让计算机执行的事情——你对我们也毫无帮助。
真实技能当然无法取代职业技能。它们能做的是放大你已经在衡量的那些东西。
想象一个拥有所有传统职业技能的团队成员：高效、熟练、经验丰富。一份能证明这一切的简历。那是个不错的基础。
现在，加上这些：敏锐、有魅力、有驱动力、专注、设定目标、鼓舞人心且有动力。慷慨、富有同理心且始终如一。一个耐心深沉的倾听者。当这样的人加入你的团队时，你的组织会发生什么？
在《哈佛商业评论》中，卢·所罗门报道，69%的管理者不愿与员工沟通。我猜其他31%中的许多人都在撒谎。
与员工沟通之所以令人不适，是因为我们建立了顺从和支配的系统，使这变得困难。我们要求人们把人性留在门外，然后用权威来改变行为。我们又将企业贪婪和短期思维，与创造有意义工作的人类渴望叠加在一起。
我们如何建立以人为本的组织，同时接受这样一个事实：我们三分之二的管理者（想必薪水丰厚、训练有素、对我们的成功不可或缺）对做自己工作的重要部分如此不适，以至于向陌生人承认了这一点？
在最近的一项调查中，研究生入学管理委员会报告称，尽管MBA在分析能力、定量专长和信息收集能力方面很强，但他们在雇主同样看重的其他关键领域严重欠缺：战略思维、书面和口头沟通、领导力和适应性。这些是互斥的吗？我们必须以牺牲一个来换取另一个吗？
所有真实技能的基础就在于此：拥有彼此交谈的信心和许可。不是去管理、贬低、恐吓或控制。仅仅是寻求被理解，并付出努力去理解对方。

readings.title: How to staycation better
body: Explain It to Me How to staycation better ﻿And why you should consider one. by Jonquilyn Hill Aug 9, 2026, 11:30 AM UTC Gift Fine Art Images via Getty Images Jonquilyn Hill is the host of Explain It to Me , your hotline for all your unanswered questions. She joined Vox in 2022 as a senior producer and then as host of The Weeds , Vox’s policy podcast. I have to be honest about something that is a great source of personal shame: I am really, really bad at taking time off of work. Despite working at a company with unlimited PTO, the last time I took a weeklong vacation was about a year ago, making me a walking cliche of the American who never goes on holiday. You could argue that the reason is cultural, that the Protestant work ethic has me in a chokehold. But I think the root cause is much simpler: For something allegedly relaxing and fun, vacations require a lot of planning and even more money. The price of flights is up, hotel rooms aren’t cheap, you need to factor in the cost of meals, and even that corny souvenir shot glass isn’t going to pay for itself. Hannah Sampson , who writes about travel for the Washington Post, says one answer is to take a staycation. “It’s taking the time to do things you normally wouldn’t do in your regular life and put on hold all of the burdensome things that you would do in your daily life,” she told Vox. “You’re enabling yourself to discover something that you might have taken for granted.” Plus, she explains, a staycation can be “really fun and rewarding while also being budget-friendly and hopefully allowing you to put money aside for the bigger trip that you want to take sometime.” So how do you make the most of a staycation? And how do you keep your typical day-to-day life from creeping in? We discuss that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sampson, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545. It sounds like the key to a successful staycation is all about mindset. How do you achieve that mindset shift? The way to really get into the staycation zone is planning and preparing and getting yourself hyped for what you’re going to do. This is something that I love about going on vacation and it applies to staying home too. Read reviews for places that you might want to go. If you’ve picked a restaurant, look at the menu and start to drool over what you’re going to eat. Think about your favorite bookstores or paths or discover a new corner of your neighborhood that you want to explore in advance. The anticipation of that experience will give you that vacation high. It’s so hard though, because you’re around the house. How do you make your home feel a little more special? I think we all got too much practice on this during the pandemic, but there are a lot of things you can do to change the vibes of your house. I have a candle that’s national park-scented, so it’s piney. In my house, we do a lot of things like use audio to set the mood. I have small kids, so we’ll play audio of a ride at Disney World or just ambient sound from a park that we like. During the pandemic, my husband and I meant to spend our anniversary at the beach where we got married, but I was pregnant. We couldn’t travel. So we found a webcam that showed the sunset on that beach and we got takeout. It was really sad, but we watched the sunset. It’s sad, but it’s also quite sweet. It’s like, “We’ll bring the beach to us.” Exactly. And it was a beautiful sunset. For me, one of the challenges of a staycation — and for all vacations, if I’m honest — is not letting real life creep in. And that’s beyond taking time to do administrative tasks around the house. That Slack goes off. I get that email. A news alert goes out and I’m just like, “Well, what if I just take a little gander?” How do you keep from letting that happen? Unplugging is so hard. You could have a couple of small kids and teach them to tell you to get off your phone, which mine have learned to do. My husband actually has a Brick device which locks your phone for you. The discipline is real there. It takes work to force yourself out of that constant need of scrolling through TikTok or just seeing what’s up at work. You don’t need to be on there. If there’s an emergency, they know how to reach you at work. So trust that process. Be super in the moment with whatever you’re doing because you need that mental break, even if you haven’t gone somewhere. You need to make the most of the time that you have, especially if you’re taking vacation time and spending it at home. Vacation time is a precious resource that you should be using to the best of your ability. ##段落
**如何更好地享受居家假期，以及为什么你应该考虑一次**  
作者：乔恩奎琳·希尔 | 2026年8月9日，上午11:30 UTC  
图片来源：Fine Art Images via Getty Images  
乔恩奎琳·希尔是《Explain It to Me》的主持人，这是你解答所有未解之谜的热线。她于2022年加入Vox，担任资深制作人，随后成为Vox政策播客《The Weeds》的主持人。

##段落
我必须坦诚一件让我深感羞愧的事：我非常、非常不擅长休假。尽管在一家提供无限带薪休假的公司工作，我上一次休一周长假大约是一年前，这让我成了“从不度假的美国人”的活生生的典型。你可能会说，原因是文化层面的，是新教工作伦理把我牢牢束缚住了。但我认为根源要简单得多：对于本应放松和有趣的事情，假期需要大量规划，更需要大把金钱。机票价格上涨，酒店房间不便宜，你还得算上餐饮开销，就连那个俗气的纪念品小酒杯也不会自己买单。

##段落
为《华盛顿邮报》撰写旅游文章的汉娜·桑普森表示，一个答案是选择居家假期。“这是花时间去做你日常生活中通常不会做的事，同时把日常生活中的繁琐事务暂时搁置，”她告诉Vox。“你让自己去发现那些你可能习以为常的东西。”此外，她解释道，居家假期可以“既真正有趣又有收获，同时还能控制预算，希望还能帮你省下钱，为将来某次更大型的旅行做准备。”

##段落
那么，如何充分利用居家假期？又如何防止日常琐事侵入其中？我们在Vox的每周听众来电播客《Explain It to Me》最新一期中讨论了这些问题及更多内容。以下是我与桑普森对话的摘录，为篇幅和清晰度做了编辑。你可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或任何你收听播客的平台收听完整节目。如果你想提交问题，请发送邮件至askvox@vox.com或致电1-800-618-8545。

##段落
听起来，居家假期成功的关键在于心态。你如何实现这种心态转变？  
真正进入居家假期状态的方法是规划、准备，并让自己对将要做的事情充满期待。这是我在外出度假时非常喜欢的一点，它同样适用于待在家里。阅读你可能想去的地方的评论。如果你选好了一家餐厅，看看菜单，开始垂涎欲滴地想象要吃什么。想想你最喜欢的书店或小径，或者提前发现社区里你想探索的新角落。对体验的期待会给你带来那种度假的感觉。

情绪高涨。但这真的很难，因为你身处家中。如何让家感觉更特别一点？我想我们在疫情期间对此都练得太多了，但确实有很多方法可以改变家里的氛围。我有一支国家公园香味的蜡烛，闻起来有松木味。在家里，我们常做很多像用音频来调节心情的事。我有小孩，所以我们常播放迪士尼乐园骑乘游戏的音频，或者我们喜欢公园的环境声。疫情期间，我丈夫和我本打算去我们结婚的海滩庆祝周年纪念，但我怀孕了，无法旅行。于是我们找到一个显示那片海滩日落的网络摄像头，还点了外卖。那真的很伤感，但我们看了日落。虽然悲伤，但也相当甜蜜。就像是“我们把海滩带到身边来。”没错，那日落很美。对我来说，居家度假的一个挑战——老实说，所有假期都一样——是别让现实生活渗入。这不仅仅是花时间做家务事那么简单。Slack消息响起来，我收到邮件，突发新闻弹出，我就想“要不要瞄一眼呢？”你怎么防止这种情况发生？断开连接真的很难。你可以有几个小孩，教他们告诉你别玩手机，我家的孩子已经学会了。我丈夫其实有个Brick设备，能帮你锁住手机。自制力确实很重要。强迫自己摆脱不断刷TikTok或查看工作动态的冲动，需要付出努力。你不需要在上面。如果有紧急情况，工作单位知道怎么联系你。所以信任这个过程。无论做什么，都要全情投入当下，因为你需要精神上的休息，即使你没去别的地方。你需要充分利用你所拥有的时间，特别是当你休假在家时。假期是宝贵的资源，你应该尽可能地利用好。查看更多：建议 给我解释 生活播客 用最新的Vox填字游戏来一场精神休息 唐纳德·特朗普有气体问题 播客 Ozempic仍无法解决的一件事 流感疫苗为何难以改进的奇怪原因 我们忽视的世界末日威胁 播客 邮箱（必填）注册 提交邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。广告内容 来自 这是原生广告的标题
